name: Name
body: Battle Forge is a monthly series that presents a new WARMACHINE scenario in each installment. Battle Forge scenarios emphasize the narrative unfolding over the course of a game and may be asymmetrical, uneven, and even somewhat experimental because the goal of Battle Forge is to create a sandbox toolset that allows for creative scenario generation and new, story-worthy experiences with WARMACHINE! Players are encouraged to modify Battle Forge scenarios in any way that makes the scenario more appropriate for their army collections and their available terrain resources. Most important of all, have fun! And if you find a better way to do something with a scenario that results in a better experience for you, let us know at feedback@privateerpress.com, so we can try it, too!

name: Name
body: Following are the key terms that will be repeated in many Battle Forge scenarios:

name: Name
body: Many scenarios utilize objectives. An objective can either be a terrain piece, a marker, or a zone designated on a terrain piece or on the map.

name: Name
body: Objective Markers are impassable terrain features and should be represented on the table with markers that are at least 20 mm in diameter. Unless otherwise specified, all Objective Markers used in a scenario should be the same size.

name: Name
body: To have more models in an area than your opponent does.

name: Name
body: An area or objective is contested if both players have models in the area or in scoring proximity to the objective at a time when scoring would take place. An area or objective is uncontested if only one player has models in the area or in scoring proximity to the objective when scoring would take place.

name: Name
body: The zone or the area of a terrain feature is held when a player occupies the area with two or more models, uncontested.

name: Name
body: An objective terrain piece or marker is secured when a player has two or more models within 1" of the objective, uncontested.

name: Name
body: Battle Forge victories can be determined by either achieving the goals of the scenario or through Victory Points, scored in a variety of ways throughout playing a scenario. Turn limits on scenarios put pressure on players to succeed within a set amount of turns, and Victory Points provide the means to determine victory when neither player has completed the primary objective of a scenario.

name: Name
body:
In addition to its standard rules, each Battle Forge scenario has two random tables that add additional Victory Point-scoring opportunities for players that vary each time the scenario is played. Mission Modifiers add additional scoring opportunities based on the position of a player’s models on the table. Achievements add additional scoring opportunities based on a player’s actions taken on the battlefield.
Players should roll a d6 to randomly determine Mission Modifiers and Achievements before the beginning of a game, or players can choose them at will if all players agree. It is recommended that only one Mission Modifier and one Achievement should be in effect during any match (unless you really want to get crazy).

name: Name
body: If a player makes an attack that destroys one or more friendly models, that player’s opponent gains 1 Victory Point. If a player makes an attack and destroys their own Leader model, that player immediately loses the match.

name: Name
body: In addition to objectives, Battle Forge scenarios will routinely draw on the following terrain elements. Dimensions provided are approximations, and you should feel free to substitute any terrain pieces you have available as necessary. Use the resources you have available to get close enough to maintain the spirit and intention of the scenario.

name: Name
body: An obstacle with an approximate footprint of 3/4" x 4". Barriers provide cover.

name: Name
body: Obstructions with an approximate footprint of 5" x 5".

name: Name
body: Forest areas with an approximate footprint of 5" in diameter.

name: Name
body: An obstacle with an approximate footprint of 2" x 2". Small obstacles provide cover.

name: Name
body: An elevated platform at least 1" above the table, such as a hill or terrace. Plateaus can possess multiple areas at different heights that models can be placed on, but the areas must be level to prevent models from falling over. If a model cannot be placed on a level area without risk of falling off, it cannot occupy that area. Models cannot be placed on slopes, and we recommend that plateau terrain with sloped surfaces not be used. Hill, Small—A plateau platform with a footprint approximately 6" in diameter and a level surface(s) at least 1" above the table that is large enough for five 30 mm models to be placed on. Hill, Large—A plateau with a footprint approximately 6" to 12" in diameter and a level surface(s) at least 1" above the table that is large enough for five 40 mm models to be placed on.

name: Name
body: An area of shallow water approximately 6" in diameter.

name: Name
body: An area of rubble approximately 6" in diameter.

name: Name
body: A 3" x 5" trench template.

name: Name
body: Battle for the spoils of a dragon’s hoard within its volcanic lair.

name: Name
body: "The Floor is Lava" is designed for 50-, 75- and 100-point forces.

name: Name
body: "The Floor is Lava" ends after six rounds.

name: Name
body: Players battle to claim the treasure hoard of a dragon from treacherous terrain that is difficult to traverse. Flyers have a distinct advantage in island hopping over the magma-filled crater, but the violent volcanic activity can make it hard for them to stay in the air.

name: Name
body:
A map has been provided, but you can set up this scenario in a variety of ways using whatever terrain you have available. The important thing is to create an environment of small land masses connected by difficult-to-pass bridges, all surrounded by deadly lava. Make sure that placement of treasure objectives is balanced for both players relative to their Deployment Zones, and ensure that flying models are advantaged for movement, albeit at increased risk when flying over the lava.
This scenario uses 9 large hills, 8 small hills, and 12 or more bridges that can span the gaps between the hills. Feel free to place obstacles as well, if space permits. The more interesting the terrain, the better.
Bridges should be 2" wide and can be cut out of sturdy cardboard, though you should also feel free to use any existing bridge terrain you have or to make them wider if you prefer. Ideally, the bridges are restrictive to movement due to their narrow dimension.
You’ll also need two each of 50 mm, 40 mm, 30 mm, and 20 mm scenario objectives as well as a small pile of treasure tokens. During setup, place two treasure tokens next to each 20 mm objective, three tokens next to each 30 mm objective, four tokens next to each 40 mm objective, and five tokens next to each 50 mm objective.

name: Name
body:
A model securing an objective at the beginning of their turn can claim one or more treasure tokens from the objective. Move the treasure tokens from the pile next to the objective to the model that claimed and will now carry them. When all of the treasure tokens have been claimed from an objective, remove the objective from the map.
A 30 mm model can carry one treasure token.
A 40 mm model can carry two treasure tokens.
A 50 mm model can carry three treasure tokens.
An 80 mm model can carry four treasure tokens.
A 120 mm model can carry five treasure tokens.
Models carrying treasure tokens cannot run and lose Stealth. A model carrying its maximum number of treasure tokens suffers –2 SPD.
If a model carrying a treasure token is destroyed or removed from play, place the treasure tokens it was carrying in a pile at the center of the location its base had occupied.
Models beginning their activation within 1" of dropped treasure tokens can claim any treasure tokens they can carry.
On any turn that a flying model moves over lava, roll a d6. On a 4–6, the model suffers the fire continuous effect. In this scenario, the fire continuous effect is cumulative, meaning a model that is already on fire can suffer an additional fire continuous effect. Separately resolve each instance of the fire continuous effect during your Maintenance Phase. Models with the fire continuous effect cannot run or charge.

name: Name
body:
Any non-flying model that moves or is moved into lava is destroyed.
Any flying model that is knocked down in lava is destroyed.
Any treasure carried by models destroyed by lava is removed from play.
A model can bank any treasure tokens it is carrying by ending its activation in its Deployment Zone. Banked treasure tokens are removed from play and kept by the player who banked them, counting them toward their final score.

name: Name
body: Roll once on both the Mission Modifiers and Achievement tables.

name: Name
body: Roll a d3 to determine the Mission Modifier for this match: 1. Gold Fever—Models carrying treasure tokens gain +1 to all attack and damage rolls but suffer –1 to DEF and ARM. 2. Wishing Well—Discard a banked or carried treasure token and roll a d6. On a roll of 4–6, choose any model in play to suffer the fire continuous effect. Discarded treasure tokens are removed from play and do not count toward victory. 3. Gold Rush—Models carrying treasure tokens can run.

name: Name
body: Roll a d3 to determine the Achievement for this match. 1. Monty Haul —The first time a treasure objective is secured during a match, roll a d6 and add that many treasure tokens to its treasure pile. Only one Monty Haul can occur per match. 2. Highwayman—The first time a player destroys an enemy model, the attacking model gains a treasure token. 3. Fool’s Gold—The second time each player claims a treasure token, that player rolls a d6. On a roll of 5 or 6, that player must discard a banked or carried treasure token.

name: Name
body: Victory conditions are checked in the following order: Decisive Win: At the end of the second player’s sixth turn, the player with the most banked and carried treasure tokens, combined, wins. Point Advantage Win: At the end of any of the second player’s turns, a player with 15 or more banked and carried treasure tokens than their opponent wins the match. Last Leader Win: At the end of any of the second player’s turns, a player with the last Leader model in play wins the match. Victory Point Win: If neither player has a Leader in play at the end of any of the second player’s turns, the player with the most banked and carried treasure tokens wins the match.
